query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under demanding service conditions, a single-phase HEA loses toughness due to stress- or thermally activated nanosegregation of key alloying elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, and Mn) to grain boundaries, which reduces GB cohesion and promotes intergranular cracking. In other words, even though the alloy is initially a homogeneous solid solution, exposure to elevated temperatures and mechanical loading leads to segregation at the GBs, causing a transition from ductile, transgranular failure to brittle, intergranular fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, homogenous (fcc) high-entropy alloy designed as a solid solution.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled grain-boundary segregation engineering treatment (for example, by inducing pre-existing Cr-rich secondary phase precipitates via heat treatment) and compare to the untreated single-phase alloy.
generation.conditions: Comparative tensile or creep tests at service-relevant intermediate temperatures (e.g., 400–700°C) and mechanical loading rates that mimic demanding engineering conditions versus tests at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries, where nanosegregation of embrittling elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) reduces cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical loading at elevated temperatures, local stresses and enhanced diffusion promote the segregation of certain principal elements to grain boundaries. This segregation decreases the cohesive strength of the GBs and induces intergranular crack initiation, thereby lowering overall toughness. An engineered variant that pre-absorbs these elements (via precipitate formation) should resist such segregation and maintain higher ductility and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The untreated single-phase HEA will show a transition from ductile transgranular fracture at ambient conditions to brittle intergranular fracture with reduced fracture toughness under service-like intermediate temperatures, while the GB‐engineered variant will retain higher toughness and ductility under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: At room temperature or mild loading conditions, the alloy exhibits ductile transgranular failure with high strength, work hardening, and excellent toughness.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where the temperature and/or stress levels are high enough to significantly accelerate elemental diffusion and segregation (e.g., intermediate service temperatures around 400–700°C and/or high strain rates or sustained loads in demanding engineering applications).
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of segregation and the quantitative extent to which GB cohesion is reduced depend on the specific alloy composition, processing history, and service environment; further investigation is needed to establish threshold conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same single-phase HEA: one as-received and one subjected to a grain-boundary engineering heat treatment designed to precipitate Cr-rich secondary phases. Conduct comparative tensile (or creep) tests at room temperature and at an intermediate temperature range (e.g., 400–700°C) under identical loading conditions. Perform post-mortem microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, and atom probe tomography) to detect GB segregation and identify fracture modes.
measurements: Fracture toughness (e.g., KJIc) from tensile or creep tests at different temperatures.
Fracture surface analysis to distinguish intergranular vs transgranular cracking.
Quantitative assessment of element segregation at grain boundaries via atom probe or high-resolution TEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the untreated and GB‐engineered samples exhibit similar fracture toughness, similar transgranular failure modes, and no significant nanosegregation differences at the grain boundaries under intermediate temperature tests, then the hypothesis that stress/temperature‐induced GB segregation is causing toughness loss would be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:GB segregation engineering to enhance ductility
cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement.
